fixes.where: weddings.html #reception-walima, 4th paragraph ('The send-off cued for the elders')
fixes.what: Name it: 'The rukhsati, vidaai or doli, as your family calls the send-off, cued for the elders; a thank-you card follows.'
fixes.why: For Pakistani and Indian families the send-off is the emotional climax of the wedding; unnamed, the line reads generic and the page's fluency drops exactly where the parents look.

fixes.where: weddings.html #anand-karaj, first paragraph ('the couple walk the four laavan')
fixes.what: Change to 'the couple circle the Guru Granth Sahib four times as the four laavan are sung'
fixes.why: The laavan are the hymns, not the walk; a Sikh parent notices the slip at once.

fixes.what: Cut 'listed / agreed / named in your proposal' from eleven occurrences to one per section (keep it in step 03 and once under Always included); replace the others with plain statements ('Signage in your languages, coordinated with your printer and the venue.')
fixes.why: Eleven hedges read as contract language, not hospitality; it undercuts 'one person to call, nothing to chase' and makes the family feel they are being limited before they have signed.

fixes.what: Add one sentence: 'If your family holds a bale-boroon or namzadi before the aghd, it goes in the programme and the elders are seated for it.'
fixes.why: The Afghan block names shirni-khori but the Persian engagement is never mentioned; Persian parents expect the aghd to sit inside that sequence.

fixes.what: Lead with the ceremonies that have no slot: 'Haldi & pheras, Anand Karaj, walima and the rukhsati: every ceremony, in its own words'
fixes.why: The three slots lean Persian/Afghan/Muslim; a Hindu or Sikh family's only cue on the home page is this one line, so it must name their days clearly.

fixes.where: index.html screen 3, Sofreh Aghd figcaption ('The Persian ceremony at the spread.')
fixes.what: Change to 'The Persian ceremony, at the sofreh.'
fixes.why: Families say sofreh; 'the spread' is the explanation, not the name, and 'at the spread' reads oddly to the very people it is written for.
